project.name: solarsim
project.description: Interactive 3D solar system visualisation for solstice and equinox education. Built with a southern hemisphere default perspective, SolarSim renders Keplerian orbital mechanics in the browser using WebGL shaders, letting users scrub through a full year to observe how Earth's axial tilt creates the seasons.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: SolarSim is an interactive 3D solar-system visualisation built to teach solstice and equinox concepts through accurate Keplerian orbital mechanics, defaulting to a southern-hemisphere perspective. The README maps the full architecture—Next.js 16, React Three Fiber, and Zustand—and explains how Sun, Earth, and Moon fit into Phase 1, giving you a roadmap for the rest of this tour.

tour.title: Application Entry Point
tour.description: The tour's code journey begins at the Next.js App Router shell. `app/page.tsx` is the server component home page that mounts the simulation inside a full-viewport `<main>`, while `app/layout.tsx` wraps every route with metadata, the PWA manifest link, and global dark-theme styles. Together they form the thin server boundary before any 3D rendering starts.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js App Router separates Server Components (like `page.tsx`, which can render on the server without client JavaScript) from Client Components marked with `'use client'`, keeping the initial HTML payload small before the WebGL canvas hydrates.

tour.title: Client Bootstrap Shell
tour.description: Building on the page entry point, `ClientRoot` is the first client boundary: it instantiates a mutable `SimulationClock` (Julian day plus rotation angle) and shares it through React context rather than Zustand, avoiding re-renders on every animation frame. It composes the 3D scene, HUD overlays, loading screen, and season-explainer controls into one coordinated shell.
tour.languageLesson: React Context is ideal here for a frequently mutated object that many descendants read but that should not trigger React reconciliation—unlike Zustand state, context value identity stays stable while the clock object's fields change in place.

tour.title: Central Application State
tour.description: The Zustand store is the single source of truth for everything the HUD and camera react to: playback speed, zoom, Earth scale, hemisphere toggle, focus target (sun, Earth, or Moon), and season-explainer overlay state. Canvas components read it via `getState()` inside `useFrame` to stay off the React render path, which is why this file ranks among the most depended-upon modules in the graph.

tour.title: 3D Scene Composition
tour.description: With state and the simulation clock in place, `Scene` is the React Three Fiber `<Canvas>` root that wires together every visible body and helper—Sun, Earth, Moon, orbit path, starfield, annotations, the frame Animator, and camera zoom sync. It owns the shared Three.js refs passed down to children, making it the highest fan-out module and the best map of the presentation layer.

tour.title: Frame Animation Engine
tour.description: The Animator runs inside R3F's `useFrame` hook each render tick: it advances the shared clock from store speeds, computes Earth and Moon positions for all three focus reference frames, handles tidal locking and nodal precession, and pushes the Sun direction uniform into Earth's shader. This is where orbital math meets the render loop—the bridge between pure functions and pixels on screen.

tour.title: Orbital Mechanics Core
tour.description: Underpinning the Animator are pure, testable functions with no React dependency. `constants.ts` centralises astronomical values—orbital elements, simulation speed bounds, Moon geometry—while `orbitalMechanics.ts` converts calendar dates to Julian days, solves Kepler's equation for Earth's position, computes sidereal rotation, and labels solstice/equinox events. These two files are among the highest fan-in domain modules because nearly every simulation feature depends on them.

tour.title: Season Explainer Domain
tour.description: SolarSim's educational mission lives in the season-explainer layer, which builds solstice and equinox event metadata, teaching copy, and deterministic camera/globe presets on top of the orbital functions from the previous step. `cameraMath.ts` supplies the Three.js viewpoint math—heliocentric framing, screen panning, and explainer-specific camera positions—so the overlay can snap learners to pedagogically meaningful views.

tour.title: HUD and Timeline
tour.description: The 2D overlay HUD sits above the WebGL canvas and is how users scrub time, toggle playback, and adjust simulation parameters. `HUD` composes the control panels and publishes a `--hud-height` CSS variable so the explainer panel can size itself, while `TimelineSlider` maps a year-scoped Julian-day range with season colour bands and solstice/equinox tick marks directly onto the mutable simulation clock.

tour.title: Explainer Overlay UI
tour.description: Connecting the domain layer to the viewport, `TopLeftControls` drives season-explainer mode—event selection, resizable overlay, and preset application—while `ZoomSync` bidirectionally links OrbitControls camera distance to the Zustand zoom store and applies explainer camera presets when teaching mode is active. This pair is where pedagogy becomes an interactive, camera-guided experience rather than static text.

tour.title: Earth Shaders and Rendering
tour.description: Earth's day/night appearance is the visual centrepiece of the season story. `Earth.tsx` loads textures and attaches a custom `ShaderMaterial`, while the paired GLSL vertex and fragment shaders compute lighting from a `uSunPositionWorld` uniform that the Animator updates each frame across all three reference frames. Understanding this pipeline explains why the globe looks correct whether you are focused on the Sun, Earth, or Moon.
tour.languageLesson: GLSL shaders run on the GPU: the vertex shader transforms mesh coordinates and passes interpolated normals to the fragment shader, which samples day/night textures and applies sun-direction lighting per pixel—far cheaper than doing the same on the CPU for every sphere point.

tour.title: PWA and Offline Support
tour.description: SolarSim is designed for classroom use without reliable connectivity. The service worker cache-first serves planet textures and hashed Next.js assets, the web app manifest declares installability, and `useOfflineStatus` exposes cache progress to the info modal. `package.json` ties it together with pnpm scripts (`dev` on port 3100, `build`, `test`, `lint`) and the dependency stack that makes the entire tour's architecture possible.
tour.languageLesson: Service workers intercept network requests in a separate thread. Cache-first strategies serve static assets instantly offline, while versioned cache names let you invalidate stale bundles without users manually clearing browser storage.
